marking_policy: Maths4U indicative marking guidance, not an official examination-board mark scheme. Award stated criteria once each, up to the part maximum. Accept valid equivalent methods. Follow-through applies only where explicitly stated; do not award an accuracy criterion for an incorrect final result.

lessons.title: Exact values, quadrants and general angles
lessons.objective: Use reference angles and coordinate signs to find exact trigonometric ratios.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: use Pythagoras and convert degrees to radians. Angles here are in radians unless a degree symbol is shown.

On the unit circle, the point at angle θ has coordinates \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\). Hence cosine is the horizontal coordinate and sine is the vertical coordinate. Their signs follow the quadrant; tangent is \(\sin\theta/\cos\theta\), defined only when cosine is nonzero.

  • At \(\pi/6\): sine is \(1/2\), cosine is \(\sqrt3/2\).
  • At \(\pi/4\): both are \(\sqrt2/2\).
  • At \(\pi/3\): sine is \(\sqrt3/2\), cosine is \(1/2\).

Sine and cosine repeat after 2π; tangent repeats after π. A reference triangle supplies magnitudes, while the quadrant supplies signs. The identity \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) does not choose a sign for a square root.

Recall later

At \(5\pi/6\), sine is \(1/2\), cosine is \(-\sqrt3/2\), and tangent is \(-1/\sqrt3\).

examples.question_html: If \(\cos\theta=-3/5\) and \(\pi/2<\theta<\pi\), find sine and tangent.
examples.solution_html: \(\sin^2\theta=1-9/25=16/25\). In quadrant II sine is positive, so \(\sin\theta=4/5\). Then \(\tan\theta=(4/5)/(-3/5)=-4/3\).

examples.question_html: Find the exact sine, cosine and tangent of \(7\pi/6\).
examples.solution_html: The reference angle is π/6 and the angle is in quadrant III. Thus sine=−1/2, cosine=−√3/2 and tangent=1/√3.

examples.question_html: Find every x in \(0\le x<2\pi\) with \(\cos x=-1/2\).
examples.solution_html: The inverse-cosine principal value is \(2\pi/3\), but cosine is also negative in quadrant III. The two angles are \(2\pi/3\) and \(4\pi/3\).

common_mistakes: Choosing a square-root sign without using the quadrant.
Treating an inverse-calculator output as every solution.
Using tangent where cosine is zero.

lessons.title: Trigonometric graphs, periods and transformations
lessons.objective: Read amplitude, midline, period, range and excluded points from a formula.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: recognise sine, cosine and tangent on a radian axis, and recall function transformations.

For \(y=a+b\sin(kx+c)\) or its cosine version, with \(b\ne0\) and \(k\ne0\), the midline is y=a, amplitude is |b| and least positive period is \(2\pi/|k|\). On the whole real line the range is \([a-|b|,a+|b|]\). A restricted domain may attain less of that range.

The inside shift is \(-c/k\), and a negative outside multiplier reflects the wave. Maximum and minimum points require both x- and y-coordinates. Endpoints count when the stated interval includes them.

Tangent has period π, is unbounded and is undefined where cosine is zero. For \(\tan(kx+c)\), asymptotes occur at \(kx+c=\pi/2+n\pi\), with integer n. Do not join a tangent graph across these gaps.

Recall later

\(y=2-5\sin(3x)\) has amplitude 5, midline y=2, period \(2\pi/3\) and whole-line range [−3,7].

examples.solution_html: The amplitude is 2, midline y=3, period \(2\pi/4=\pi/2\), and range [1,5]. The value at x=0 is 3.

examples.question_html: Find the range and period of \(y=-1+3\cos(x/2)\).
examples.solution_html: The range is [−4,2]. The inner multiplier is 1/2, so the period is \(2\pi/(1/2)=4\pi\), not π.

examples.question_html: Find the period and asymptotes of \(y=\tan(2x)\).
examples.solution_html: The period is π/2. The excluded points satisfy \(2x=\pi/2+n\pi\), so \(x=\pi/4+n\pi/2\). Each is a vertical asymptote.

common_mistakes: Using the inside multiplier itself as the period.
Confusing the vertical shift with the amplitude.
Connecting tangent branches or counting an excluded endpoint.

lessons.title: Identities, factorisation and valid domains
lessons.objective: Transform trigonometric expressions while retaining every domain restriction.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: simplify fractions and factor a product without losing a zero factor.

The core relations are \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\) for real x and \(\tan x=\sin x/\cos x\) where \(\cos x\ne0\). Dividing the first identity by cos²x gives \(1+\tan^2x=1/\cos^2x\) only on that same domain.

In a proof, start with one side and transform it into the other using valid equalities. An identity holds at every point of its stated domain; an equation may hold only at selected angles. A cancellation can simplify a formula without filling a hole in the original domain.

If sin x or cos x is a factor in an equation, check its zero case before division. Multiplying by a denominator or squaring can admit extra candidates, so check solutions in the original expression.

Recall later

\((1-\cos^2x)/\sin x=\sin x\) when \(\sin x\ne0\); the original quotient is still undefined at x=0.

examples.question_html: Simplify \((1-\sin^2x)/\cos x\) and state its restriction.
examples.solution_html: Replace the numerator by cos²x and cancel one cosine: the result is cos x, with the original restriction \(\cos x\ne0\), or \(x\ne\pi/2+n\pi\).
Group one sin²x+cos²x pair: \((\sin^2x+\cos^2x)+\cos^2x=1+\cos^2x\). No division is used, so this identity is valid for every real x.

examples.question_html: Solve \(2\sin x\cos x=\sin x\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
examples.solution_html: Factor \(\sin x(2\cos x-1)=0\). The first factor gives x=0,π; the second gives x=π/3,5π/3. Dividing by sine would lose the first two solutions.

common_mistakes: Cancelling a factor without retaining its excluded values.
Dividing an equation by sine or cosine and losing roots.
Using a chain of implications in place of valid equalities in an identity proof.

lessons.title: Trigonometric equations on a stated interval
lessons.objective: Find all angle branches, using the full transformed interval and the original domain.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: use exact values and inverse functions, and recognise each ratio's period.

For integer n, if \(\sin u=a\) and α=arcsin a, the families are \(u=\alpha+2n\pi\) and \(u=\pi-\alpha+2n\pi\). If \(\cos u=a\) and α=arccos a, use \(u=\pm\alpha+2n\pi\). These require |a|≤1. Duplicate angles at extreme values are counted once.

For \(\tan u=a\), use \(u=\arctan a+n\pi\), retaining excluded cosine-zero values. Calculator inverses return principal values, not a complete interval solution.

The principal output ranges are \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\) for arcsine, \([0,\pi]\) for arccosine, and \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\) for arctangent.

When u=kx+c, transform the entire x-interval into a u-interval first, find every branch in it, and transform back. Reverse inequalities if dividing by a negative coefficient. Check open/closed endpoints and substitute candidates into the original equation.

Recall later

\(\cos x=0\) has x=π/2,3π/2 on \(0\le x<2\pi\); \(\tan x\) is undefined at those same points.

examples.solution_html: The reference angle is π/3. Sine is negative in quadrants III and IV, giving \(x=4\pi/3,5\pi/3\).
The doubled angle runs through \(0\le2x<4\pi\). It has values π/3,5π/3,7π/3,11π/3. Dividing by 2 gives x=π/6,5π/6,7π/6,11π/6.
Tangent is zero at integer multiples of π. Thus x=π/6+nπ. The permitted values are π/6 and 7π/6.

common_mistakes: Solving for 2x only between 0 and 2π when x spans that interval.
Mixing a degree period with radian inputs.

lessons.title: Trigonometric equations that become quadratics
lessons.objective: Solve a polynomial in one ratio, reject impossible ratio values and recover all angles.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: factor quadratics or use the quadratic formula, and solve basic trigonometric equations.

Substitute u=sin x, cos x or tan x to isolate the algebraic step. Solve for every u, then reject values outside [−1,1] for sine/cosine. Tangent can take every real value where it is defined.

Use sin²x+cos²x=1 to replace mixed squared ratios before forming the quadratic. Each admissible u still requires all appropriate angle branches. Two quadratic roots do not necessarily produce four angles: u=±1 gives only one sine angle per turn, and an impossible u gives none.

Finally check the original equation and interval, especially if you divided by a ratio, cleared a denominator or squared an expression.

Recall later

If an algebraic step gives \(\cos x=2\), reject it: no real angle has that cosine.

examples.solution_html: \((2\cos x+1)(\cos x-1)=0\). The values cos x=−1/2 or 1 give x=2π/3,4π/3 or 0. The endpoint 2π is excluded, so there are three solutions.
The factorisation is (sin x−1)(sin x−2)=0. Reject sin x=2; sin x=1 gives the sole solution x=π/2.
Take both signs: tan x=±√3. The four permitted angles are π/3,2π/3,4π/3,5π/3, none at a tangent asymptote.

common_mistakes: Taking only the positive square root of a squared ratio.
Counting a duplicated endpoint or assuming two angles for an extreme sine value.

problems.title: A quadrant determines the sign
problems.objective: Use a given cosine and quadrant to recover exact ratios and a rational expression.
problems.hint_html: Pythagoras gives the magnitude of sine. The stated quadrant determines its sign.

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sin\theta\) exactly.
parts.solution_html: sin²θ=1−25/169=144/169. In quadrant II sine is positive, so sin θ=12/13.

criteria.requirement: Obtain sin²θ=144/169 or the corresponding reference-triangle length.
Choose the positive value 12/13 using the quadrant.

parts.alternative_methods: A 5–12–13 reference triangle with a correct sign argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving both square-root signs despite the stated quadrant.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\tan\theta\) exactly.

criteria.requirement: Use sine divided by cosine.
Give −12/5.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct reference-triangle ratio with the quadrant sign is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using cosine divided by sine.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Evaluate \((1-\sin\theta)/\cos^2\theta\) exactly.
parts.solution_html: The numerator is 1/13 and the denominator is 25/169, so the quotient is (1/13)(169/25)=13/25. The denominator is nonzero. Equivalently the quotient is 1/(1+sin θ).

criteria.requirement: Obtain the correct numerator and squared denominator.
Divide the fractions correctly or use a valid identity.
Give the exact result 13/25.

parts.alternative_methods: Rationalising with the Pythagorean identity is accepted on this valid domain.
parts.common_error: Squaring the denominator ratio incorrectly or changing its sign.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Related angles from one reference triangle
problems.objective: Use periodicity and quadrant signs without introducing an angle-addition formula.
problems.stem_html: The angle α is acute and \(\sin\alpha=3/5\). Define \(\beta=\pi+\alpha\).
problems.hint_html: Use the 3–4–5 reference triangle and track the quadrant of each related angle.

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\cos\alpha\) and \(\tan\alpha\) exactly.
parts.solution_html: Acuteness gives cos α=√(1−9/25)=4/5. Hence tan α=(3/5)/(4/5)=3/4.

criteria.requirement: Give cos α=4/5 with the acute sign.
Give tan α=3/4.

parts.alternative_methods: A labelled reference triangle is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the negative square root for an acute angle.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\sin\beta\) and \(\cos\beta\) exactly.
parts.solution_html: β is in quadrant III with reference angle α, so both sine and cosine are negative: −3/5 and −4/5.

criteria.requirement: Give sin β=−3/5.
Give cos β=−4/5.

parts.alternative_methods: A unit-circle half-turn argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping the quadrant-I signs after a half-turn.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Evaluate \(\tan\beta+\sin(\pi-\alpha)\) exactly.
parts.solution_html: Tangent has period π, so tan β=3/4. The supplementary angle has sine 3/5. Their sum is 3/4+3/5=27/20.

criteria.requirement: Obtain tan β=3/4.
Obtain sin(π−α)=3/5.
Add to give 27/20.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct quadrant/reference-angle argument for both terms is accepted.
parts.common_error: Assuming the sum of two different ratios must itself lie between −1 and 1.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A reflected cosine wave
problems.objective: Read graph features and find exact level crossings with included endpoints.
problems.stem_html: Let \(f(x)=2-3\cos(2x)\) for real x. In parts (b) and (c), consider \(0\le x\le\pi\).
problems.hint_html: The negative coefficient swaps the positions of cosine maxima and minima, but the amplitude stays positive.

parts.prompt_html: State the amplitude, least positive period and range of f.
parts.solution_html: The amplitude is |−3|=3, the period is 2π/2=π, and the outputs run from 2−3=−1 to 2+3=5.

criteria.requirement: Give amplitude 3.
Give period π.
Give range [−1,5].

parts.alternative_methods: A correctly transformed cosine graph is accepted.
parts.common_error: Reporting a negative amplitude or period 2π.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Give all maximum and minimum points on the stated interval.
parts.solution_html: Cos(2x)=1 at x=0 and π, giving both included minima. Cos(2x)=−1 at x=π/2, giving the maximum (π/2,5).

criteria.requirement: Identify both included minimum points (0,−1) and (π,−1).
Identify maximum (π/2,5).
Justify the positions using the extreme cosine values or an equivalent graph argument.

parts.alternative_methods: A labelled graph with the endpoint status clear is accepted.
parts.common_error: Omitting the minimum at the included endpoint x=π.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Solve \(f(x)=2\) on the stated interval.
parts.solution_html: The equation reduces to cos(2x)=0. For 0≤2x≤2π, the doubled angles are π/2 and 3π/2, so x=π/4 and 3π/4.

criteria.requirement: Reduce to cos(2x)=0 and use the doubled-angle interval.
Give both solutions π/4 and 3π/4.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct midline-crossing graph argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving the doubled angles as the x-values.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Reconstructing a sine model
problems.objective: Recover parameters and count crossings on a half-open interval.
problems.stem_html: A function \(g(x)=a+b\sin(kx)\), with a,b,k positive, has maximum 7, minimum −1 and least positive period \(2\pi/3\).
problems.hint_html: The midline is the average of the extreme values; the amplitude is half their difference.

parts.prompt_html: Find a, b and k.

criteria.requirement: Give a=3.
Give b=4.
Give k=3.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent midline/range/period equations are accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the full output range width as the amplitude.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Give the y-intercept and the first maximum point with x>0.
parts.solution_html: At x=0, sine is zero, giving (0,3). The first positive maximum has 3x=π/2, so it is (π/6,7).

criteria.requirement: Give y-intercept (0,3).
Give first positive maximum (π/6,7).

parts.alternative_methods: A correct quarter-period graph argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using x=π/2 without accounting for the inner multiplier.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find every x with \(g(x)=3\) on \(0\le x<2\pi\), and state how many there are.
parts.solution_html: Sin(3x)=0, so x=nπ/3. The half-open interval allows integers n=0,1,2,3,4,5. There are six roots; n=6 gives the excluded endpoint 2π.

criteria.requirement: Use x=nπ/3 or an equivalent zero-crossing method.
List exactly the six permitted x-values.
State six roots and respect the excluded endpoint 2π.

parts.alternative_methods: A complete, correctly indexed list from the graph is accepted.
parts.common_error: Counting 2π as a seventh root.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A simplified formula with missing points
problems.objective: Simplify a quotient, solve on its original domain and explain removable holes.
problems.stem_html: Define \(E(x)=(1-\cos^2x)/\sin x\) wherever this expression is defined.
problems.hint_html: Use the Pythagorean identity before cancelling. The cancellation does not change the original denominator restriction.

parts.prompt_html: Simplify E(x) and state every excluded real x.
parts.solution_html: The numerator is sin²x, so E(x)=sin x after cancelling on sin x≠0. The excluded values are x=nπ for integer n.

criteria.requirement: Simplify to sin x.
Retain the full exclusion x=nπ, n integer.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct statement of the same sine-zero set is accepted.
parts.common_error: Claiming the quotient is defined at all real x after cancellation.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Solve \(E(x)=1/2\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
parts.solution_html: On the permitted domain solve sin x=1/2. The candidates are π/6 and 5π/6; both have nonzero sine and satisfy the original quotient.

criteria.requirement: Reduce the original equation to sine equal to 1/2 on its valid domain.
Find both angles π/6 and 5π/6.
Check that both satisfy the original domain/expression.

parts.alternative_methods: Direct substitution into the quotient is accepted.
parts.common_error: Adding a denominator-zero angle as a solution.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Explain why E and the function x↦sin x are not the same function on the whole real line. Give a specific example.
parts.answer_html: The domains differ; E(0) is undefined while sin 0=0.
parts.solution_html: A function includes its domain. At x=0 the quotient is 0/0 and is undefined, while the sine function has value zero. They agree on E’s domain, but sine extends it to the missing points.

criteria.requirement: Explain the difference in domains.
Give a correct specific missing point, such as x=0 or π.

parts.alternative_methods: Any integer multiple of π is a valid example.
parts.common_error: Treating 0/0 as zero.
parts.label: c

problems.title: An identity and a legitimate division
problems.objective: Prove a conditional identity and check a zero case before dividing an equation.
problems.hint_html: Replace tangent by sine over cosine. In part (b), test cos x=0 before dividing by cos²x.

parts.prompt_html: Prove \((1+\tan^2x)\cos^2x=1\) wherever the left side is defined.
parts.solution_html: On cos x≠0, use tan x=sin x/cos x. Expanding gives (1+sin²x/cos²x)cos²x=cos²x+sin²x=1, using the Pythagorean identity.

criteria.requirement: Use tangent as sine divided by cosine on cos x≠0.
Simplify the product to cos²x+sin²x.
Conclude 1 by the Pythagorean identity with the valid domain retained.

parts.alternative_methods: Dividing the Pythagorean identity first and then multiplying on the same domain is accepted.
parts.common_error: Treating the expression as defined when tangent is undefined.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Solve \(\sin^2x=3\cos^2x\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
parts.solution_html: If cos x=0, the equation would be 1=0, so that case gives no solution. Otherwise divide by cos²x to get tan²x=3. Both signs tan x=±√3 give the four listed angles.

criteria.requirement: Check the cosine-zero case or avoid division with an equivalent identity method.
Obtain both tangent signs or an equivalent complete ratio condition.
Give all four permitted angles.

parts.alternative_methods: Using 1−cos²x=3cos²x, then cos x=±1/2, is accepted.
parts.common_error: Taking only tan x=+√3 or silently losing a zero-denominator case.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Identify the excluded x-values for the expression in part (a) on \(0\le x<2\pi\), and explain why simplification does not restore them.
parts.solution_html: The left side contains tangent, so the cosine-zero values π/2 and 3π/2 remain excluded. The simplified constant 1 is an extension at those points, not a value of the original expression.

criteria.requirement: List π/2 and 3π/2.
Explain the original tangent/domain restriction remains after simplification.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent domain explanation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Substituting an undefined tangent and then multiplying it by zero.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A shifted, doubled sine argument
problems.objective: Transfer the full interval, find all branches and transform back.
problems.hint_html: Let u=2x−π/6 and transform the interval before listing the sine branches.

parts.prompt_html: State the interval for \(u=2x-\pi/6\).
parts.solution_html: Doubling gives 0≤2x<4π. Subtract π/6 from both ends: −π/6≤u<23π/6.

criteria.requirement: Transform both interval endpoints.
Give the correct half-open interval [−π/6,23π/6).

parts.alternative_methods: A correct numerical interval in radians with exact endpoint meanings is accepted.
parts.common_error: Restricting u to a single turn.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: List every u in this interval with sin u=1/2.
parts.solution_html: The two families are u=π/6+2nπ and u=5π/6+2nπ. The stated interval retains n=0 and n=1 for each family, giving the four values.

criteria.requirement: Use both correct sine solution families.
Retain the values from the additional turn.
Give exactly the four permitted u-values.

parts.alternative_methods: A complete interval graph argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using only a principal arcsine value.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Hence find all x-solutions.
parts.solution_html: Use x=(u+π/6)/2 for each candidate. The four values are π/6,π/2,7π/6,3π/2. All lie in the original interval and give sine 1/2 in the original equation.

criteria.requirement: Apply x=(u+π/6)/2 to all candidates.
Give all four valid x-values.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent exact representations are accepted.
parts.common_error: Forgetting to undo the phase shift before dividing by two.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Tangent: period, exclusions and a false rule
problems.objective: Solve a shifted tangent equation and disprove an invalid distributive claim.
problems.hint_html: Tangent has period π. It does not distribute over addition in its argument.

parts.prompt_html: Find the excluded x-values in the stated interval.
parts.solution_html: Tangent is undefined when x+π/4=π/2+nπ, so x=π/4+nπ. The two exclusions are π/4 and 5π/4.

criteria.requirement: Use the cosine-zero condition for the shifted argument.
Give both exclusions π/4 and 5π/4.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct asymptote argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Excluding the unshifted tangent asymptotes instead.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Solve the original equation.
parts.solution_html: x+π/4=−π/4+nπ gives x=−π/2+nπ. The interval retains x=π/2 and 3π/2; neither is an excluded input of this shifted function.

criteria.requirement: Use a correct tangent family and undo the shift.
Give exactly π/2 and 3π/2.

parts.alternative_methods: Using the family 3π/4+nπ for the argument is equivalent.
parts.common_error: Rejecting π/2 merely because unshifted tan x is undefined there.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: A student claims \(\tan(x+\pi/4)=\tan x+1\). Use x=π/3 and signs to show this is not an identity.
parts.answer_html: At x=π/3, the left side is negative and the right side is positive.
parts.solution_html: The left argument is 7π/12, in quadrant II, so its tangent is negative. The right side is √3+1>0. Both sides are defined and have different signs, so the proposed identity is false.

criteria.requirement: Identify the left argument 7π/12 and its negative tangent sign.
Show the right side √3+1 is positive.
Conclude the defined values differ, giving a valid counterexample.

parts.alternative_methods: Correct evaluated numerical values at this same input are accepted.
parts.common_error: Using an undefined input as if it supplied two comparable values.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A quadratic in sine with three roots per turn
problems.objective: Factor in a ratio and count an extreme sine level correctly.
problems.hint_html: Let u=sin x. An extreme sine value has only one angle in a half-open full turn.

parts.prompt_html: Factor the quadratic and state the possible sine values.
parts.solution_html: With u=sin x, 2u²+u−1=(2u−1)(u+1). Thus u=1/2 or −1, both in the sine range.

criteria.requirement: Obtain the correct factorisation.
State both admissible sine values.

parts.alternative_methods: The quadratic formula is accepted.
parts.common_error: Assuming a quadratic always gives four trigonometric angles.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Solve for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
parts.solution_html: Sin x=1/2 gives π/6 and 5π/6. Sin x=−1 gives only 3π/2 in this interval. There are three distinct roots.

criteria.requirement: Give both roots for sine 1/2.
Give the single root for sine −1.
State the complete distinct solution set on the interval.

parts.alternative_methods: A graph intersecting the two admissible sine levels is accepted.
parts.common_error: Listing a second copy of the same minimum-angle root.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: How many solutions are there for \(0\le x\le4\pi\)? Justify the endpoint count.
parts.answer_html: Six; neither 0 nor 4π is a root.
parts.solution_html: The equation has period 2π, so two full turns give six roots. The endpoints have sine zero and make the original left side −1, so including 4π adds no root. The second-turn roots are 13π/6,17π/6,7π/2.

criteria.requirement: Use the 2π period to obtain two sets of three roots.
Give six and correctly check the included endpoints.

parts.alternative_methods: A complete list of six valid roots is accepted.
parts.common_error: Adding a seventh root solely because the upper endpoint is included.
parts.label: c

problems.title: An impossible cosine root
problems.objective: Use an identity to form a quadratic, filter its roots and recover both real angles.
problems.hint_html: Replace sin²x by 1−cos²x. Check every algebraic cosine value against [−1,1] before taking an inverse.

parts.prompt_html: Show that \(u=\cos x\) satisfies \(3u^2-3u-1=0\).
parts.solution_html: Substitution gives u(2u−3)=1−u². Expanding and collecting yields 3u²−3u−1=0.

criteria.requirement: Use sin²x=1−cos²x.
Expand and collect the quadratic terms.
Obtain 3u²−3u−1=0.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent correct rearrangement is accepted.
parts.common_error: Replacing sin²x by 1−cos x without the square.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find both algebraic u-roots and identify which is admissible.
parts.solution_html: The quadratic formula gives u=(3±√21)/6. The plus value is approximately 1.26376>1, so cannot be a real cosine. The minus value is approximately −0.263763, inside [−1,1].

criteria.requirement: Give both exact quadratic roots.
Reject the plus root using the cosine range and retain the minus root.

parts.alternative_methods: Exact inequalities instead of decimal comparisons are accepted.
parts.common_error: Applying arccos to a value larger than one.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all x-solutions to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_html: For c=(3−√21)/6, the principal angle is arccos c≈1.837717212. The second angle is 2π−arccos c≈4.445468095. Both satisfy the original equation and interval, giving 1.84 and 4.45 rad to 3 significant figures.

criteria.requirement: Obtain the principal radian angle from the exact admissible root.
Find the second branch 2π minus that angle.
Give both solutions correctly rounded to 3 significant figures with the original domain respected.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent inverse-cosine notation followed by correct rounding is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping only the principal inverse value or switching calculator units to degrees.
parts.label: c
